latin.330: GAR. Ego vero vix oculis meis credidi cum legerem facultatem genitricem inter facultates morales locum habere posse: An etiam ut eam physicis & medicis tanquam male fidei possessoribus ereptam, moralis philosophia in posterum sibi tanquam proprium peculium vindicet? Quid vero habet facultas ista, quare potius ad moralium dignitatem evehi debeat, quam concoctrix, vel altrix, vel augmentatrix, quas hactenus docuerunt Philosophi non esse rationis participes, sed natura sua brutas ac sui nescias, quaeque homini conveniant, non qua homo est, sed qua naturam habet cum aliis animalibus communem? Denique quae lex erit Decalogi, cuius praecepto facultas generandi subjacere credenda sit? Moralia enim Decalogo circumscribi omnes, ut spero, consentiunt. At saltem moralibus subjecta est. Imo neque hoc simpliciter verum, alioqui ex imperio voluntatis semper moveretur, quod saepe aliter fieri certum. Neque foemina semper vel concipit, cum vult, vel non concipit, quando non vult.
latin.331: PLAC. Egone simpliciter dixi, facultatem genitricem esse facultatem moralem? tantum dixi: corruptionem naturae universalis cum esset, etiam ipsam facultatem genitricem, quatenus moralis quaedam facultas est, corrupisse. Significavi igitur non absolute moralem esse, sed quodam respectu. Tribus autem modis spectari potest, uno, ut est facultas quaedam seu proprietas generica: quo modo spectata facultas est animae vegetativae mere physica & bruta: nihilque intendit gignere, nisi rem vegetantem. Altero, ut est facultas animalis moliens generationem animalis, atque adeo ipsius animae sensitivae productionem: quomodo dici potest facultas animae sensitivae, cuius appetitu sensitivo excitatur ad generandum, & applicatur. Denique spectari potest ut est facultas hominis pendens aliquomodo non solum ab appetitu sensitivo, sed etiam a voluntate, & intendens generationem non canis, aut leonis, aut alius animalis bruti, sed hominis. Eatenus dici potest moralis, quatenus elaborat semen ut producatur animal rationale praeditum facultatibus moralibus, & excitatur ac applicatur ad eam rem facultatibus moralibus, voluntate & appetitu sensitivo.
latin.332: Sicut ergo appetitus sensitivus, quamvis genere suo nonnisi sensitivus sit, tamen in homine spectari potest, quatenus est aliquo modo rationalis, &, ut loquitur Aristoteles, logou metechon, atque ita & virtutis capax est, & lege regi potest; Sic facultas generatrix, licet generice spectata nullo modo moralis sit, tamen quatenus est facultas hominis, cuius & appetitu aliquomodo regitur, & generationem molitur, quid est cur eatenus moralis aliquomodo dici non possit? Id quod ipse vir doctus innuere satis videtur cum ait, eam imperio voluntatis saepe non moveri: concedere enim videtur, eam imperio voluntatis aliquando moveri. Quid est igitur quamobrem eatenus non possit appellari moralis? Nihil igitur aliud volui, nisi eam quatenus ab appetitu seu libidine dependet, & elaborat semen accommodate ad facultates morales, eatenus corruptam fuisse, atque, ut ratione naturae tendit ad productionem hominis, sic ratione corruptionis tendit ad productionem hominis corrupti. Quid est ea in re, dignum tam acri reprehensione? Est quidem facultatis generatricis, si secundum rationem illam suam genericam spectetur, eadem quae altricis, aut auctricis ratio: non vero, si secundum specificam, quam habet in homine, cuius ab appetitu dependet. Non enim concoctrix qua concoctrix, aut altrix qua altrix ullo modo dependet a voluntate, sed tantum per accidens, quatenus utraque cibi sumptionem sequitur pendentem a voluntate. Sed generatio qua talis aliquomodo in potestate est voluntatis seu appetitus: Nam nec generant unquam patres non concurrente appetitu, & possunt a generando etiam perpetuo abstinere si velint. Quid igitur est, cur, ut manducandi, sic generandi facultas lege regi non possit? Et quo pertinet mandatum Decalogi, non concupisces?
latin.333: GAR. Verum his missis, quid est, quod dicitur Adae corruptio convertisse facultatem generatricem ad generationem tanquam finem ultimum? Nam illa certe corruptio, cum sit universalis, alias etiam facultates infecit non minus quam istam. Quidni ergo caeteras facultates ad actus suos, concoctricem ad concoctionem, altricem ad nutritionem, &c. tanquam finem ultimum convertisse dicatur? ut sit pro facultatum numero etiam finium ultimorum numerus. Quod quis ferat eorum qui norunt finem ultimum homini non posse esse nisi unum?
latin.334: PLAC. Et universalis est illa corruptio, & alias etiam facultates infecit, sed ad propositum sola generans faciebat, quia de propagatione hominis, per quam propagatur illa corruptio, agebatur. Sed neque, ut jam monui, concoctio & nutritio sunt, ut actus generandi, infecti libidine, & facultas generandi caeteras facultates conatur quales sunt, propagare. Interim certum est non tam perfecte suas obire functiones concoctricem & altricem post peccatum admissum quam ante: itaque morbis variis & morti, etiam ab infantia omnes sunt obnoxii homines, nec tamen concoctio aut nutritio sunt ultimi fines, sed subordinati tantum conservationi individui & propagationi speciei. Finis ultimus verus non potest esse nisi unus, nimirum Deus. Sed finis ultimus falsus genere tantum unus est, specie autem & numero multiplex; vel enim voluptas quaeritur, vel utilitas, vel honor, horumque etiam pro variis rebus in quibus quaeruntur, magna est varietas.
latin.335: GAR. Praeterea, Cum finis ultimus relationem habeat ad fines intermedios & subalternos, eorum erit proprie finis ultimus, qui finium subalternorum, & ultimi distinctionem nosse possunt: quod cum neque in corruptionem universalem illam, neque in facultatem generatricem, aut aliam simpliciter physicam convenire possit, quomodo dicetur facultas genitrix a corruptione converti ad generationem tanquam ad finem ultimum? Distinguendum potius fuerit inter facultatem, & hominem, qui facultate utitur. Hic enim poterit sane intelligentia ac voluntate sua finem ultimum sibi praestituere: sed ipsa facultas physica, finem habet ad quem ab Autore naturae determinata est, quem semper respicit, quicquid homo corruptus moliatur, ut concoctrix concoctionem, genitrix generationem, &c. PLAC. Si bene ratiocinatur vir doctus sola mens agit propter finem, non voluntas: haec enim non cognoscit proprie, nedum ut distinctionem cognoscat inter finem ultimum & subordinatos.

pass_a.330: GAR can hardly trust his eyes reading that the generative faculty belongs among morals—will moral philosophy also snatch it from physicists and physicians as from bad-faith possessors and claim it as her peculiar? What has that faculty that it should be raised to moral dignity above the concoctive, nutritive, or augmentative powers which philosophers have taught are not partakers of reason but by nature brute and unaware of themselves, belonging to man not as man but as sharing nature with other animals? Finally, what Decalogue law is the generative faculty to be under? All agree morals are bounded by the Decalogue. Subject to morals at least? Not even that is simply true: otherwise the will's empire would always move it, which often fails—nor does a woman always conceive when she wills, or not conceive when she does not.
pass_a.331: Placeus denies he called the generative faculty simply moral. He said only that universal corruption of nature corrupted even that faculty insofar as it is somehow a moral faculty—so not absolutely moral, but in a respect. Three ways of viewing it: first, as a generic vegetative property, merely physical and brute, aiming only to beget a vegetal thing; second, as an animal faculty attempting animal generation and sensitive-soul production, stirred by sensitive appetite; third, as a human faculty depending also on will and aiming at a man, not a dog or lion. So far it is moral as it works seed for a rational animal endowed with moral powers and is excited by will and sensitive appetite toward that work.
pass_a.332: As man's sensitive appetite can be viewed as somehow rational and law-governable—Aristotle's partaking of reason—so the generative faculty, though not moral in genus, can be moral insofar as it is a human faculty ruled by appetite and attempting generation. GAR himself hints it is sometimes moved by will when he says it often is not. Placeus meant only that, as depending on lust and fitting seed to moral powers, it was corrupted—tending by nature to a man, by corruption to a corrupt man. Viewed generically it matches nutritive or augmentative; viewed as specific to man depending on appetite it does not. Concoctive and nutritive depend on will only accidentally via food; generation as such is somehow in appetite's power—fathers never generate without appetite and can abstain forever. So generating, like eating, can be under law—and under the Decalogue's 'You shall not covet.' Bound that way the faculty is not yanked from physics; it is only marked as humanly ruleable where appetite and seed meet moral powers.
pass_a.333: GAR sets the moral-faculty fight aside and asks: if Adam's corruption turned the generative faculty to generation as a last end, and that corruption is universal, why not say it also turned the concoctive to concoction and the nutritive to nutrition as last ends—yielding as many last ends as faculties? Who who knows man's last end can be only one would bear that? The quarrel then is not whether generation is somehow moral, but whether Placeus multiplies last ends by the number of corrupted powers.
pass_a.334: Placeus grants the corruption is universal and hit other faculties, but for this debate only the generative mattered, because the issue was propagation of man, the path by which the corruption spreads. Concoction and nutrition are not lust-infected like generating; the generative tries to propagate other faculties as they are. After sin those faculties work less perfectly—hence disease and death from infancy—yet they remain subordinate ends for conserving the individual and propagating the species, not last ends. The true last end is only God; a false last end is one in genus but many in species and number—pleasure, utility, honor, and their many objects. So the many-last-ends scare does not force Placeus to make every vegetative work a rival summum bonum.
pass_a.335: GAR adds: a last end properly belongs to those who can know the distinction of subaltern ends and the last—which fits neither universal corruption nor a merely physical generative faculty. Better distinguish the faculty from the man who uses it: he can set a last end by intellect and will, but the physical faculty keeps the end Nature's Author fixed—concoction, generation, and so on—whatever the corrupt man attempts. Placeus: if that reasoning holds, only the mind acts for an end, not the will, which does not properly know, much less know last versus subordinate ends. Tip into the fuller reply on faculties and false ends, where pleasure versus generation is pressed harder.

330: GAR. But I scarcely trusted my eyes when I read that the generative faculty could have a place among the moral faculties: Will moral philosophy also snatch it hereafter from the physicists and physicians as from possessors of bad faith, and claim it as her own peculiar? What has that faculty, that it ought rather to be raised to the dignity of morals than the concoctive, or nutritive, or augmentative, which philosophers have hitherto taught are not partakers of reason, but by their nature brute and unaware of themselves, and which belong to man not as he is man, but as he has a nature common with other animals? Finally, what law of the Decalogue is there to whose precept the faculty of generating is to be believed subject? For all, I hope, agree that morals are bounded by the Decalogue. But at least it is subject to morals. Nay, not even that is simply true; otherwise it would always be moved by the empire of the will, which it is certain often happens otherwise. Nor does a woman always either conceive when she wills, or not conceive when she does not will.
331: PLAC. Did I simply say the generative faculty is a moral faculty? I only said: that the corruption of nature, being universal, corrupted even the generative faculty itself, insofar as it is a certain moral faculty. I therefore meant not that it is absolutely moral, but in a certain respect. And it can be viewed in three ways: first, as a certain faculty or generic property: so viewed it is a faculty of the vegetative soul, merely physical and brute, and aims to beget nothing but a vegetal thing. Second, as an animal faculty attempting the generation of an animal, and so the production of the sensitive soul itself: so it can be called a faculty of the sensitive soul, by whose sensitive appetite it is excited and applied to generating. Finally it can be viewed as a faculty of man depending somehow not only on the sensitive appetite but also on the will, and aiming at the generation not of a dog or lion or other brute animal, but of a man. So far it can be called moral, insofar as it works seed that a rational animal endowed with moral faculties may be produced, and is excited and applied to that by the moral faculties—will and sensitive appetite.
332: Just as therefore the sensitive appetite, though in its genus only sensitive, yet in man can be viewed insofar as it is somehow rational and, as Aristotle says, partaking of reason, and so is capable of virtue and can be ruled by law; so the generative faculty, though generically viewed in no way moral, yet insofar as it is a faculty of man, by whose appetite it is somehow ruled and which attempts generation—why can it not so far be called somehow moral? Which the learned man himself seems to hint enough when he says it is often not moved by the empire of the will: for he seems to concede that it is sometimes moved by the empire of the will. Why then can it not so far be called moral? I meant nothing else than that insofar as it depends on appetite or lust, and works seed suited to the moral faculties, it was so far corrupted, and as by nature's reason it tends to producing a man, so by reason of corruption it tends to producing a corrupt man. What in that is worthy of so sharp a rebuke? Indeed for the generative faculty, if viewed by that generic account of it, there is the same reason as for the nutritive or augmentative; but not if viewed by the specific account it has in man, on whose appetite it depends. For the concoctive as concoctive, or nutritive as nutritive, in no way depends on the will, but only accidentally, insofar as each follows the taking of food which depends on the will. But generation as such is somehow in the power of will or appetite: for fathers never generate without appetite concurring, and they can even abstain from generating perpetually if they will. Why then can the faculty of generating, like that of eating, not be ruled by law? And to what does the Decalogue's command, You shall not covet, pertain?
333: GAR. But these things set aside, what is this—that Adam's corruption turned the generative faculty to generation as to a last end? For that corruption, being universal, infected the other faculties no less than this one. Why then should it not be said to have turned the other faculties to their acts—the concoctive to concoction, the nutritive to nutrition, &c.—as to a last end? so that for the number of faculties there would also be a number of last ends. Which of those who know that man's last end can be only one would bear that?
334: PLAC. And that corruption is universal, and infected the other faculties too, but for the purpose only the generative one mattered, because the matter was the propagation of man, through which that corruption is propagated. But neither, as I already noted, are concoction and nutrition, like the act of generating, infected with lust, and the generative faculty tries to propagate the other faculties as they are. Meanwhile it is certain the concoctive and nutritive do not perform their functions as perfectly after sin was committed as before: and so all men from infancy are liable to various diseases and death; yet concoction and nutrition are not last ends, but only subordinate to the conservation of the individual and the propagation of the species. The true last end can be only one, namely God. But a false last end is one only in genus, and multiple in species and number; for either pleasure is sought, or utility, or honor, and of these also, for the various things in which they are sought, there is a great variety.
335: GAR. Further, since a last end has relation to intermediate and subaltern ends, properly that will be a last end for those who can know the distinction of subaltern ends and the last: which, since it can fit neither that universal corruption nor the generative faculty or any other simply physical one, how will the generative faculty be said to be turned by corruption to generation as to a last end? Distinguishing rather between the faculty and the man who uses the faculty would have been better. For he can indeed by his understanding and will set himself a last end: but the physical faculty itself has the end to which it was determined by the Author of nature, which it always regards, whatever the corrupt man attempts—as the concoctive concoction, the generative generation, &c. PLAC. If the learned man reasons well, only the mind acts for an end, not the will: for the will does not properly know, much less know the distinction between the last end and the subordinate ones.
